audit_items.title: Supporting Check: Can an attacker trigger division by zero through specific cell withholding patterns?
audit_items.state_context: 50% threshold check in MinimumColumnCountToReconstruct() guards the call. Coset shift by RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR=7 (BLS12-381 primitive root) mathematically prevents zero divisors.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The Go wrapper delegates all polynomial arithmetic (FFT, coset evaluation, polynomial division) to ckzg4844 C library. The C library implements coset FFT with RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR=7, the BLS12-381 primitive root of unity. The coset {7*omega^k} is mathematically disjoint from all roots of the vanishing polynomial Z(x) because 7 is not in any root-of-unity subgroup generated by omega. The Go layer enforces a 50% threshold check before calling the C library. Error propagation: all C errors are wrapped and returned as Go errors.
state_anomalies_found: No division-by-zero path reachable from external input
50% threshold check at Go layer correctly bounds the missing cell count
assert() in C library's recover_cells() at recovery.c:261 would cause SIGABRT if triggered, but is protected by an equivalent C-side threshold check, making it unreachable from external input
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of recovery results. Each reconstruction is performed fresh.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: errgroup pattern used for parallel per-blob recovery. Error from any goroutine causes overall failure. No shared mutable state during computation.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Mathematical proof: vanishing polynomial Z(x) = product_{j in missing}(x - omega^j). Evaluated on coset: Z(7*omega^k) = product_{j in missing}(7*omega^k - omega^j). For a zero factor: 7*omega^k = omega^j, meaning 7 = omega^{j-k}. Since 7 is a primitive root of BLS12-381 (order r-1) and omega generates a subgroup of order 8192 (power of 2 dividing r-1), the element 7 is NOT in the subgroup generated by omega. Therefore Z(7*omega^k) != 0 for all k and all valid missing cell choices. No counterexample exists.
attack_scenarios: Withhold maximum allowed cells (just below 50%): Z has maximal roots on standard domain, none on coset — division is always safe
Withhold cells to maximize clustering of vanishing polynomial roots: still cannot bring a root onto the coset
Provide cells with invalid indices: rejected by C library input validation before any division occurs

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Attacker can control which cells are withheld (P2P layer), thus controlling missing cell indices passed to recovery. Despite full control over vanishing polynomial roots, the coset design unconditionally prevents zero divisors. The 50% threshold at the Go layer also prevents recovery from being attempted with insufficient cells.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker controls missing cell selection but cannot cause division by zero due to coset design.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: Invariant: Z(7*omega^k) != 0 for all k and all valid missing cell sets. Proof: 7 (BLS12-381 primitive root) is not in any subgroup of order 2^n, so the coset {7*omega^k} is disjoint from the standard evaluation domain {omega^j}. The invariant holds unconditionally. The 50% threshold is a guard for reconstruction uniqueness, not for zero-divisor prevention.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Coset shift by RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR=7 (BLS12-381 primitive root of unity in Montgomery form)
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient. The coset design is mathematically sound and unconditionally prevents zero divisors regardless of which cells are missing.
edge_cases: All cells present: no missing indices, vanishing polynomial is constant 1, no division by zero
Exactly one cell missing: Z is linear with one root on standard domain, never on coset
Maximum missing cells (just below 50%): Z has many roots on standard domain, none intersect the coset

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Division by zero via cell withholding is mathematically impossible. The coset FFT design using the BLS12-381 primitive root 7 unconditionally prevents the vanishing polynomial from evaluating to zero at any coset point. The 50% threshold check provides defense-in-depth at the Go layer. No vulnerability exists.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. Consider adding a comment in the code explaining the mathematical basis for the coset design's safety against division by zero.

audit_items.reasoning: The coset FFT design using RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR=7 (BLS12-381 primitive root) mathematically prevents division by zero for any valid attacker-chosen missing cell pattern. The 50% threshold guard at the Go layer provides additional defense-in-depth. No exploitable vulnerability exists.

audit_items.title: Supporting Check: Does the validator node have defensive error handling for unexpected division by zero?
audit_items.state_context: C library error codes: C_KZG_OK, C_KZG_BADARGS, C_KZG_ERROR, C_KZG_MALLOC. Go bindings translate non-OK codes to Go errors. Process-terminating assert() exists but is protected by C-side threshold check.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: Error handling analysis across layers: (1) Go wrapper correctly checks err != nil and wraps errors; (2) errgroup collects first error from parallel goroutines and returns it to caller; (3) ReconstructDataColumnSidecars returns error to caller (data_columns_reconstruct.go or ReconstructBlobs); (4) Callers log and handle errors without panicking. No crash path via error returns. One identified concern: assert() in recovery.c would cause SIGABRT (not caught by Go's panic/recover), but this is unreachable from external input.
state_anomalies_found: assert() in recovery.c (line ~261) causes process termination via SIGABRT — not a Go error, not catchable by recover()
fr_div with zero divisor produces unspecified field element (silent incorrect result, not an error return) — not reachable in practice
Both anomalies are protected by pre-condition checks that make them unreachable from external input
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching affects error handling correctness.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: errgroup correctly aggregates errors from parallel goroutines. First non-nil error is returned; other goroutines continue to completion or error independently.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Path analysis for crash scenarios: (1) assert() path: requires C-side num_cells < CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB after Go-side 50% threshold check has already passed. Since MinimumColumnCountToReconstruct() >= CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB/2 >= CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB threshold in C, the Go check passing implies the C check also passes, making assert() unreachable. (2) fr_div zero path: mathematically impossible as shown in CHK-0151 analysis. (3) All other error paths (invalid input format, malloc failure) correctly propagate as Go errors.
attack_scenarios: Trigger SIGABRT via assert(): blocked by equivalent C-side threshold check
Trigger silent wrong result via fr_div(x, 0): blocked by coset design
Trigger Go panic via nil pointer in error path: no nil dereferences found in error path
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: No race conditions in error handling path.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Error returns from C library propagate cleanly through Go wrapper to caller. The only dangerous path (SIGABRT from assert) is unreachable. The fr_div silent-zero path is mathematically unreachable. All externally-triggerable errors result in graceful Go error returns.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker can trigger error returns (graceful), but not crashes or silent wrong results.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: Invariant 'all division-by-zero scenarios either return a Go error or are unreachable from external input' holds. The error handling chain is complete: C_KZG_BADARGS -> Go error -> errgroup error -> ReconstructDataColumnSidecars error -> caller handles gracefully. The assert() crash path and fr_div zero path are both unreachable. No defensive zero-check before division is needed given the mathematical guarantees.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: 50% threshold in Go (MinimumColumnCountToReconstruct), equivalent threshold in C (num_cells < CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB), coset design (RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR=7)
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Guards are sufficient for all externally-reachable inputs.
edge_cases: C_KZG_MALLOC error: propagated as Go error, no crash
LoadTrustedSetup not called: Go bindings panic at startup (not P2P-triggered)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Error handling for division-by-zero scenarios is complete and correct. All externally-reachable code paths return Go errors that are handled gracefully. The assert() crash path and silent zero result path are both unreachable from external input. No exploitable vulnerability.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Code quality improvement: consider replacing the assert() in recovery.c with a proper error return (C_KZG_ERROR) for defense-in-depth. This prevents future code changes from accidentally creating a crash path. This is not a security fix.

audit_items.reasoning: Error handling is complete and correct. All externally-reachable paths produce graceful Go error returns. The assert() crash path in the C library is unreachable from external input due to equivalent pre-condition checks. Minor recommendation: replace assert() with error return for defensive coding best practice.

audit_items.title: Invariant Falsification: Can coset_fft_field shift_factor deviate from PRIMITIVE_ROOT_OF_UNITY through any state transition or initialization path?
audit_items.state_context: RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR is a C static const in fft.c. No API parameter for shift factor. KZGSettings struct has no shift factor field. LoadTrustedSetup generates roots of unity from the same primitive root.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR is defined as a C static const fr_t in fft.c — a compile-time constant representing 7 in BLS12-381 Montgomery form. This constant is baked into the binary and cannot be modified at runtime by any external input, API call, configuration option, or state transition. The Go bindings do not expose any parameter to alter the shift factor. KZGSettings (the trusted setup) is loaded once at process start and does not contain or configure the shift factor. The roots of unity in KZGSettings are generated independently from ROOT_OF_UNITY (also 7) in setup.c.
state_anomalies_found: None. The shift factor is immutable by language semantics (C static const).
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: Not applicable. The constant is a compile-time value, not a cached computed result.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Read-only constant — no concurrency issues possible.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Complete enumeration of state transition paths: (1) Initialization: LoadTrustedSetup() sets KZGSettings for roots of unity but does not touch RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR; (2) ComputeCellsAndKZGProofs(): passes blob data, shift factor is constant; (3) RecoverCellsAndKZGProofs(): passes cell indices and cell data, shift factor is constant; (4) All other kzg.go functions: none interact with shift factor. No symbolic path exists that modifies RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR. The constant's value (7 in Montgomery form) has been independently verified: 0x0000000efffffff1 is the first limb of 7 in BLS12-381 Montgomery form (7 * 2^256 mod r).
attack_scenarios: Pass crafted cell data to influence shift factor: impossible — cell data is processed independently of the constant
Call LoadTrustedSetup with malicious parameters: Go bindings validate the trusted setup; shift factor is not a parameter
Memory corruption to overwrite .rodata: outside protocol threat model, requires OS-level exploit
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None. Constant cannot change at any time.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: No external interface can influence RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR. It is not part of any API, configuration, or state. The invariant RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR == 7 (in BLS12-381 Montgomery form) holds unconditionally throughout the process lifetime.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Zero attack surface for this property.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant holds trivially by C language semantics. A C static const cannot be modified after compilation. The value 7 in Montgomery form (0x0000000efffffff1...) is the correct BLS12-381 primitive root of unity. INV_RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR (the modular inverse of 7 mod r) is also hardcoded correctly. Both constants are verified correct by the c-kzg-4844 library's test suite.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: C language static const qualifier prevents runtime modification
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Trivially sufficient. No runtime path can bypass a C compile-time constant.
edge_cases: Recompilation with different FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_EXT_BLOB: RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR (=7) remains valid as a primitive root of the full BLS12-381 multiplicative group, not specific to any subgroup
Different trusted setup file: shift factor is not read from the trusted setup file

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The shift factor (RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR=7) is a compile-time C constant that cannot be altered at runtime via any state transition, initialization path, or external input. The invariant holds trivially. No vulnerability exists.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. The constant is correctly set to the BLS12-381 primitive root of unity.

audit_items.reasoning: RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR is a compile-time C constant equal to 7 in BLS12-381 Montgomery form. No runtime path, state transition, or attacker-controlled input can modify this value. The invariant holds unconditionally.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-001/tb-002/tb-003: Is the bit-reversal permutation (brp) correctly implemented as an involution?
audit_items.state_context: BRP is applied internally in C library. Go code provides cell indices and cell data as input. BRP is applied to: (1) input cells in encoding (data_fr before FFT), (2) input cells in recovery (cells_brp before IDFT), (3) output data in recovery (reconstructed_data_out after IDFT). Consistency between encoding and recovery is critical.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The bit_reversal_permutation in utils.c implements the mathematical bit-reversal permutation (BRP) for FFT ordering. Key properties: (1) Single-pass in-place swap with condition r > i ensures each pair swapped exactly once; (2) log2_pow2(n) correctly computes log2 for powers of two; (3) reverse_bits is a 64-bit bit reversal; (4) right-shift by unused_bit_len extracts the b-bit reversal from the 64-bit reversal. The BRP is used consistently in both ComputeCellsAndKZGProofs and RecoverCellsAndKZGProofs, applied to internal data arrays after index validation.
state_anomalies_found: n == 0 input returns C_KZG_BADARGS — correctly handled

n == 1 input causes log2_pow2 to return 0, then unused_bit_len = 64, triggering assert(unused_bit_len <= 63) — but n=1 is rejected before the assert is reached by the n == 0 check actually (n >= 2 required)
These edge cases are not reachable with standard EIP-7594 parameters (FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_EXT_BLOB=8192, CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB=128)
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching. BRP is computed in-place each call.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Thread-safe: each call operates on a distinct memory region. No shared state.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Mathematical proof of involution: the b-bit bit-reversal function rev_b satisfies rev_b(rev_b(x)) = x for all x in [0, 2^b). This is proven by: (1) bit reversal is a bijection on {0,...,2^b-1}; (2) applying it twice restores the original value (each bit position is swapped twice). The implementation's r > i condition ensures no element is moved twice in a single pass — exactly the elements where r < i are not moved (their counterpart at position r is moved to them when i == r and r < i was false). Fixed points where r == i (self-symmetric elements like 0 and 2^{b-1}) are never swapped. Consistency: encoding applies BRP to data_fr before computing FFT coefficients; recovery applies BRP to the input cells array and to the output reconstructed array. This is symmetric by design.
attack_scenarios: Provide cell indices in non-bit-reversed order to confuse recovery: the C library maps cell indices to BRP positions internally, so order of provided indices does not affect correctness
Provide duplicate cell indices: C library validates uniqueness and returns C_KZG_BADARGS
Provide out-of-range cell indices (>= CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB): validated and rejected
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None. BRP is deterministic and has no timing-dependent behavior.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The BRP is an internal algorithm step applied to fixed-size arrays determined by FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_EXT_BLOB and CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB. Attackers can provide cell data and indices, but the BRP is applied to internal arrays after input validation. The BRP correctness is determined by the implementation, not by attacker input.
entry_points: Internal to C library (not directly attacker-controlled)
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: BRP is applied internally; attacker cannot influence which BRP is used or how it is applied.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: Invariant: bit_reversal_permutation applied twice returns the original array (involution property). Proven by: (1) Mathematical identity rev_b(rev_b(x)) = x for all x; (2) Implementation correctly implements rev_b via reverse_bits(x) >> (64-b); (3) r > i condition prevents double-swapping in a single pass; (4) Applying the function twice therefore restores the original array. The BRP is used consistently between encoding and recovery, maintaining the correct round-trip property for cells and polynomial coefficients.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: r > i swap condition, is_power_of_two(n) validation, n >= 2 requirement
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Guards ensure the mathematical preconditions for the involution property are satisfied.
edge_cases: n = 2: elements 0 and 1 both map to themselves (0=rev_1(0), 1=rev_1(1) in 1-bit reversal) — no swaps, correctly handled
n = 4: element 1 maps to 2 (01->10 in 2-bit reversal), element 2 maps to 1 — correctly swapped
n = 8192: all 8192 elements handled correctly by the general algorithm

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The bit-reversal permutation is correctly implemented as a mathematical involution. The implementation in utils.c correctly computes the b-bit reversal for all elements, applies each swap exactly once via the r > i condition, and handles all valid input sizes. No inconsistency exists between the encoding and recovery applications of BRP. No vulnerability.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. Consider adding a comment referencing the EIP-7594 specification for the BRP usage to improve code documentation.

audit_items.reasoning: The bit-reversal permutation is correctly implemented as an involution in the c-kzg-4844 C library. The mathematical proof holds unconditionally for all power-of-two sizes. The BRP is applied consistently between encoding and recovery. No exploitable bug in the BRP implementation was found.

audit_items.title: Can division by zero polynomial be triggered via crafted missing cell indices in divide_polynomialcoeff?
audit_items.state_context: Vanishing polynomial Z(x) is constructed from missing cell roots: Z(x) = prod_{j in missing}(x - omega^j). Division is performed at coset points {7*omega^k}. Missing cell set is determined by which cells the attacker withholds. 50% threshold limits the maximum number of missing cells.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The divide_polynomialcoeff step in the EIP-7594 specification corresponds to element-wise division of (P*Z) by Z over the coset in the c-kzg-4844 implementation. The divisor at each coset point is Z(7*omega^k) = product_{j in missing_brp}(7*omega^k - omega^j). An attacker controls which cells are missing, thus controlling the set of roots of Z. However, the mathematical structure of the coset prevents any root of Z from coinciding with any coset evaluation point.
state_anomalies_found: fr_div documentation notes zero divisor behavior is 'unspecified' — but this path is mathematically unreachable
No explicit zero-check before fr_div in recovery.c — reliance on mathematical impossibility
If missing_indices is empty (all cells present), no division is performed (fast path taken)
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: Vanishing polynomial is constructed fresh for each recovery call. No caching.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Each goroutine in ReconstructDataColumnSidecars handles one blob independently. No shared state in the division computation.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Complete mathematical analysis: Let S be any attacker-chosen set of missing cell indices (|S| <= NumberOfColumns/2). The vanishing polynomial is Z(x) = product_{j in BRP(S)}(x - omega^j) where BRP is the bit-reversal permutation (a bijection on cell indices). The coset evaluation: Z(7*omega^k) = product_{j in BRP(S)}(7*omega^k - omega^j). For a zero factor: 7*omega^k = omega^j. This requires 7 = omega^{j-k} mod p. Since omega has order FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_EXT_BLOB = 8192 = 2^13, any element omega^m has order dividing 8192. But 7 is the BLS12-381 primitive root with order r-1 = 2^32 * ... (not a power of 2, and specifically 7^8192 != 1 mod r since 7 has full order r-1). Therefore 7 is NOT in the subgroup generated by omega, and 7 != omega^m for any integer m. This proves Z(7*omega^k) != 0 for all k and all valid S.
attack_scenarios: Choose missing indices to maximize roots of Z closest to coset: still cannot place a root on the coset by the group-theoretic argument
Provide exactly 1 cell (maximum missing = NumberOfColumns - 1): Z has maximal roots but none on the coset
Provide cells with indices {0, 2, 4, ..., NumberOfColumns-2} (all even indices): all standard-domain roots are at omega^{BRP(odd)} positions, none equal to 7*omega^k for any k
Choose S such that BRP(S) consists entirely of indices whose omega values are 'close to' coset points in field arithmetic: mathematical proof shows no BRP(S) can achieve this

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Attacker has full control over which cells are withheld from P2P (up to the 50% threshold), directly controlling the missing cell index set S and thus the roots of Z. Despite this full control over the vanishing polynomial's roots, the coset design provides a mathematically unconditional barrier. The group-theoretic proof holds for any choice of S, including adversarially chosen S.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker controls the vanishing polynomial's roots but cannot place them on the coset evaluation points.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: Invariant: for all valid missing cell sets S and all k in [0, FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_EXT_BLOB), Z(7*omega^k) != 0. Proof: (1) 7 is the BLS12-381 primitive root with order r-1; (2) omega is a primitive FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_EXT_BLOB-th root of unity (order 8192 = 2^13); (3) The subgroup H = {omega^k : k in [0, 8192)} has order 8192; (4) The coset 7H = {7*omega^k} is disjoint from H because 7 is not in H (since 7^8192 != 1 mod r); (5) The roots of Z(x) are all in H (they are omega^j for various j); (6) Therefore no root of Z lies in 7H; (7) Therefore Z evaluates to a nonzero field element at every point in 7H. QED.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: Coset design: RECOVERY_SHIFT_FACTOR=7 (BLS12-381 primitive root) creates coset 7H disjoint from H (standard evaluation domain)
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: The coset design alone is mathematically sufficient to prevent zero divisors for any valid missing cell set. The 50% threshold ensures recovery uniqueness but is not needed for zero-divisor prevention.
edge_cases: S is empty (all cells present): Z(x) = 1 (constant), Z(7*omega^k) = 1 != 0. Fast path taken, no division performed anyway.

S = {all cells} (impossible due to 50% threshold): mathematically Z would be the full FIELD_ELEMENTS_PER_EXT_BLOB-degree polynomial with roots at all of H. Z(7*omega^k) = product_{j in [0,8192)}(7*omega^k - omega^j). This equals a nonzero value since the coset is disjoint from H.
|S| = 1 (one cell missing): Z is linear, one root in H, evaluates nonzero on 7H.
|S| = NumberOfColumns/2 - 1 (maximum allowed by 50% threshold): Z has maximal roots in H, all nonzero on 7H by the proof.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Division by zero polynomial cannot be triggered via any crafted missing cell index pattern. The group-theoretic proof is unconditional: for any nonempty proper subset S of cell indices, the vanishing polynomial Z(x) with roots at {omega^j : j in BRP(S)} evaluates to a nonzero field element at every coset point {7*omega^k}. The mathematical basis is the disjointness of the coset 7H from the standard evaluation domain H, which holds by the group structure of BLS12-381. No bug exists.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. The design is mathematically sound. Consider adding a brief comment in recovery.c explaining why the fr_div cannot produce a zero denominator, to aid future code reviewers.

audit_items.reasoning: A complete group-theoretic proof shows that Z(7*omega^k) != 0 for all k and all valid missing cell sets. The proof relies on 7 being the BLS12-381 primitive root (not in any root-of-unity subgroup), making the coset 7H disjoint from the standard evaluation domain H. Attacker control over missing cell indices cannot overcome this mathematical barrier.
